::: {.essay-lede}
The formula $e^{i\pi}+1=0$ looks almost ceremonial. Its derivation, however, is a straightforward and exceptionally useful consequence of the power-series definition of the exponential function.
:::

## Start with a power series

For every complex number $z$, the exponential function is defined by the absolutely convergent series

$$
e^z=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{n!}.
$$

Put $z=ix$ for real $x$. Because powers of $i$ repeat in a cycle of length four, we can group even and odd powers:

$$
\begin{aligned}
e^{ix}
&=\left(1-\frac{x^2}{2!}+\frac{x^4}{4!}-\cdots\right)\\
&\quad+i\left(x-\frac{x^3}{3!}+\frac{x^5}{5!}-\cdots\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

The real and imaginary parts are precisely the Taylor series of cosine and sine. Thus

$$
e^{ix}=\cos x+i\sin x.
$$ {#eq-euler}

## Evaluate at a half-turn

A half-turn corresponds to $x=\pi$. Since $\cos\pi=-1$ and $\sin\pi=0$, equation @eq-euler becomes

$$
e^{i\pi}=-1,
$$

or, in its most familiar form,

$$
\boxed{e^{i\pi}+1=0}.
$$

## The geometrical meaning

For real $x$, the complex number $e^{ix}$ lies on the unit circle. Varying $x$ traces a rotation. Exponentials, trigonometry, and complex multiplication turn out to be different descriptions of the same structure.
